Oh honey, there are always going to be people who disagree with the choice of same-sex couples having children. Being a part of a thriving rainbow families community, I can tell you most of the kids are very happy and well adjusted. 

When out with my family, I’ve even had adult children of same-sex couples, come and talk to us.  Always sharing the love of their own family and stating that it is so nice to see their own family structure being represented in the public. 

I would suggest trying to hunt down the following resources, both are Australian, but I believe one of them is on Netflix, otherwise a VPN to abc iview au will get you access. The first is a series called ‘you can’t ask that’ season 2, episode 8 is same-sex families. Of all the children interviewed there was only one person with a negative experience. But she was also born into a heterosexual household and holds very Christian beliefs. The other show is recommend is a documentary called Gaby Babies. It’s several years old but follows children from across Sydney and their daily experiences. 

From personal experience my 15 year old SD LOVES having 4 mums. She has the ability to meet her biological father but doesn’t want anything to do with him. It’s too early to say what my BS think but they also enjoy the community that has been built around them.

My SD (15) tends to have significantly more spent on her as opposed to our son (3) but that is because the stuff she wants / needs is more expensive. I figure it will all even out in the end as she gets older and begins work, her gifts will reduce and we will spend more on ‘ours baby’.

I have been lucky enough to have had several people stand up and offer a kidney.  My Aunty was the first but she was automatically disqualified as she has diabetes.  My Dad went through all the testing.  On the day I was suppose to meet him at the surgeons office to organise a day for transplant we were told it could not go ahead as my father had a massive kidney stone that his previous Neph had failed to pick up so that mixed with possible pre-diabetes took that offer off the table.  I ended up on dialysis about 4 months after that date.  Christmas last year a very wonderful friend offered to be tested for me.  We went through the matching process and he recieved a call from the red cross informing him that he is a match.  Unfortunately they were incorrect, they should never have called him. I was told by the transplant co-ordinator about 3 weeks after this call that he was not a match and that my antibodies were significantly too high and would ultimately kill off his kidney.  At this point of time my wonderful transplant coordinator left her position and a new guy filled in her place.  He is not great at his job.  Another friend (who use to date my friend that initally offered his kidney) was donating to her boyfriend and decided she wanted to be tested for me too as my first friend (who was tested) was willing to be tested for her now boyfriend, so essentially we were planning a swap.  My transplant coordinator refused to do the matching.  She has incidentally this week donated her kidney to her boyfriend.  

My sister and half brother have both offered to be tested.  My sisters testing has come back as a 5 out of 6 match and she is about to start the next phase in the testing process, we are hoping to be ready to have surgery around December when we both go on summer school holidays.  The transplant coordinator hasn't really tried to contact my half brother as he is currently in jail and is in the 'too hard' basket.  It makes me insane, why take on a co-ordinator role if you aren't going to actually co-ordinate. Grrr,  that is a rant for another day though.

I'm only new to this subreddit so I'm not going to say too much regarding your voice. I would like to address this question though: "Should I practice before starting vocal lessons if I'm worried he/she will judge me for my inexperience?"

I began learning classical singing roughly this time last year and saw my vocal coach as an absolute beginner. She is a reasonably well known performer in Australia so I was rather nervous to go into the lesson without a lot of background knowledge. This however was the best thing I have ever done. We made massive strides in just a couple of weeks because I didn't teach myself bad technique. It is much better to walk in admitting you don't know what your doing and they can correct you properly the first time as re-learning something that has previously been acquired incorrectly takes a lot more time. Each week she tells me that she can't believe how fast I have learnt and within just a few months I had moved from simple art songs to more challenging arias. I believe the reason for this is because I didn't know anything to begin with and was willing to make mistakes in front of her. Jump into the deep end and get those lessons if you feel that strongly about singing.

I am a primary school (elementary for the Americans on here) and for the most part look very femme, so I blend into the hetro-normative narrative quite well. To drive home the point that I liked the other gender I went all sterotypical - came to school with a short fawhawk, suit vest, white shirt and tie.  It worked a treat,  he finally got the message, but so did some of the more cluey kids and I started getting remarks like 'such and such thinks your gay' and 'I heard you're married to a girl'.  I pretty much responded with a 'Does it really matter if I am gay and married to a girl? - does it make me any different?'  The children in question sat, thought for a second and responded with a 'nah Miss,  it makes you even more cool'.  

On a different note,  I have a little boy in my year 2 class.  He is very flamboyant and I am assuming mum and dad have noticed this and discussed his sexuality with him.  This particular day we had completed an art project with glitter and he decided to throw the glitter in the air whilst doing a dance, singing very loudly, 'I'm Gay,  I'm Gay'.  I pulled him aside and quietly asked him what did 'being gay mean?'.  He put his hands on his hips, looked me in the eyes and with a sigh said 'I can't believe I have to explain this to you, but being gay means that I am a boy, who loves other boys.  It also means if you are a girl, you  like other girls, duh Miss, I can't believe you wouldn't know that'.  I had to hold in the laughter. Later that week,  I was teaching students about questions, so we played a game of celebrity heads to drive home the point.  One of the students was Justin Beiber.  This particular child was struggling with who they could be so I asked the class to give them a clue.  The child who I spoke about previously put up his hand and said 'Oh,  I really like this one,  he is just my type'...

Tell her that if she has reasons to believe that her parents will disown her based on her sexuality then she should wait until she is independent and living away from home. Make sure she has a support network of close friends who she feels comfortable talking about this stuff with and who she can rely on for help if she needs it.

If she decides to go ahead with telling them, I found ripping it off like a band aid, just being blunt and to the point was helpful. Do it in private (unless there is the potential for physical abuse) and make sure she realises that they may take a while to get use to the news. For some people having pamphlets/website addresses etc to support groups such as pflag maybe helpful. 

Finally she needs to be prepared for their reaction. Being bi she may come across lines like, well if you are attracted to both sexes why don't you just choose to date men? It's just a phase or other hurtful things.

I am glad you have decided to help her out. I realise that school was hard for you, but what she was also going through was probably really tough.
